title: ThreadX 5.6 → 6.5, Cortex-M4 → M85
subtitle: One application, three migration stages, executable evidence

blocks.text: The same Clang-built application runs on the real ThreadX 5.6 kernel, then on current MIT ThreadX 6.5, then is built for Cortex-M85.
Use ← / →, touch arrows, or swipe. Home returns here.

title: Change one thing per stage
subtitle: So every difference has exactly one cause

rows: Cortex-M55: newest core this QEMU runs

items: Stage 1 → 2 isolates the RTOS migration on the core the TX5 kernel was built for.
Stage 2 → 3 isolates the CPU port change on an unchanged kernel release.
M55 shares the Armv8.1-M port family with M85, so it is the closest runnable proxy, not a substitute for M85 execution.

blocks.text: The float ABI change in stage 1 → 2 is forced by the TX5 archive, not chosen. It is called out as its own diff later.

title: ThreadX 5 and 6: what actually changes
subtitle: Same service model; different delivery, port contract and licence

rows: Headers + prebuilt GCC archive, no kernel source
Commercial; SDK copy restricted to WICED use
M4, M55, M85 and many more
Hard-float; FPU context in the port
Fixed by archive: errno extension, no error checking

blocks.text: Rows are findings from this specific SDK archive and its headers. Other licensed TX5 distributions may have been built with different options.

title: Where the ThreadX 5 kernel comes from
subtitle: TX5 was never open source; the WICED SDK ships it as binaries

items: The public WICED SDK 3.1.0 contains ThreadX 5.6 headers and ThreadX.ARM_CM4.release.a.
Its README restricts those objects to WICED use, so nothing from the SDK is in this repository.
The build links the archive from TX5_ROOT, a separate checkout; configuration fails if TX5_ROOT is inside the repository.
CI clones the same SDK commit into the runner's temp directory for every run.

blocks.text:
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout \
    https://github.com/wwwllllllll/bcm-wiced-sdk.git $TX5_ROOT
git -C $TX5_ROOT sparse-checkout set --no-cone '/WICED/RTOS/ThreadX/'
git -C $TX5_ROOT checkout 0886ec932a063e12db768cd09428e8a8ab555bce
# ThreadX.ARM_CM4.release.a sha256:
# 71288b46e58b2c398118674b53feb708994e18740cf7e5d68bc8d070f72fac1e
blocks.label: Reproducible external dependency, identified by commit and hash

title: Reading a binary-only kernel
subtitle: No source, so inspect build attributes, symbols and machine code

blocks.text:
$ llvm-readelf -A tx_thread_create.o
  CPU_name: Cortex-M4        CPU_arch: ARM v7E-M
  ABI_enum_size: Packed      (no ABI_VFP_args, no FP_arch)
$ llvm-nm tx_thread_schedule.o
  T __tx_PendSVHandler   T __tx_SVCallHandler
  U tx_low_power_enter   U _tx_thread_system_stack_ptr
$ llvm-strings tx_thread_initialize.o
  ThreadX Cortex-M3/GNU Version G5.6.5.2
blocks.label: Actual inspection of the WICED ThreadX.ARM_CM4.release.a members

items: No VFP tag: the archive is soft-float, so every object in the image must be soft-float.
Packed enums: GCC -fshort-enums; Clang must match it.
The CM4 archive is the Cortex-M3 port: it never saves FPU registers.
Unresolved WICED hooks show exactly what the board layer must provide.

title: The exact versions, not moving targets
subtitle: Every kernel input is pinned and identifiable

rows: Eclipse ThreadX v6.5.2.202603_rel, latest observed on 2026-10-11

blocks.text: The originally linked v6.1.12_rel tag carries Azure RTOS hardware-linked licence text in its own tree; it is not substituted for the MIT release.

title: Cortex-M4, M55 and M85
subtitle: Keep CPU architecture distinct from a particular microcontroller

rows: TX5 and TX6 run on MPS2 AN386

blocks.text: Core IP features and SoC implementations vary. A new core does not bring the old board's GPIO, clocks, memory addresses, DMA or wiring with it.

title: The most modern runnable QEMU Cortex-M here
subtitle: Probe the installed executable instead of relying on development docs

blocks.text:
qemu-system-arm --version
qemu-system-arm -machine help
qemu-system-arm -cpu help
# installed: 11.1.0
# present: mps2-an386 / cortex-m4, mps3-an547 / cortex-m55
# absent:  mps3-an555 / cortex-m85
blocks.label: Actual local inventory, saved in evidence/qemu-*.txt

blocks.text: M55 is the newest Cortex-M CPU exposed by this installed QEMU build. QEMU development documentation mentions AN555, but it is not in the tested binary.
An M85 image is never run under an M55 CPU and labelled M85. The M85 ELF remains a separate, explicitly unexecuted build artifact.

title: Licensing is an engineering input
subtitle: Public on GitHub does not mean free to redistribute

items: The WICED SDK README limits its ThreadX / NetX objects to use with WICED.
The TX5 archive and headers are linked from an external checkout and never committed or published.
The application, board layer, adapter and tests are independently written; original work is MIT.
ThreadX 6.5 is pinned as an MIT submodule with its upstream notices.
PDF typography embeds Roboto under OFL 1.1, with the notice shipped beside the PDF.

blocks.text: This is an engineering demonstration, not a legal opinion on WICED licence scope. Product use of a TX5 kernel needs its own licence.

title: The source trees
subtitle: The TX5 kernel stays outside; the repository holds only original work

blocks.name: source-trees
blocks.caption: Left: what TX5_ROOT must contain. Right: the public repository.

blocks.text: TX5-only and TX6-only files are small and named for their stage: one adapter, one board hook, one tx_user.h.

title: Migration workflow
subtitle: Change one dimension at a time

blocks.name: workflow
blocks.caption: Kernel first on the original core, then the core on the new kernel.

blocks.text: Stages 1 and 2 give a like-for-like Cortex-M4 run on each kernel. Stage 3 then needs only the CPU port change.

title: What really executes
subtitle: No mock RTOS, no fake emulator success

blocks.name: architecture
blocks.caption: Clang-built firmware runs the real TX5.6 or TX6.5 scheduler under QEMU.

blocks.text: The board adapter virtualizes two LEDs and deterministic active-low buttons. It does not emulate or access a physical GPIO controller.

title: Diff 1: how each kernel enters the build
subtitle: Imported binary archive vs rebuilt source

blocks.text:
# Stage 1: cmake/tx5-wiced-adapter.cmake
- add_library(threadx STATIC IMPORTED GLOBAL)
- IMPORTED_LOCATION  ${TX5_ROOT}/.../ThreadX.ARM_CM4.release.a
- INTERFACE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS  TX_INCLUDE_USER_DEFINE_FILE
- include dirs: ver5.6/ and ver5.6/Cortex_M3_M4/GCC/
# Stages 2-3: CMakeLists.txt
+ set(THREADX_ARCH ${TX_CORE})        # cortex_m4 / m55 / m85
+ set(TX_USER_FILE config/tx6/tx_user.h)
+ add_subdirectory(third_party/threadx)
# all stages
  target_link_libraries(threadx_gpio_demo PRIVATE threadx)
blocks.label: Actual build integration; the application target is identical

blocks.text: With source, the kernel is recompiled for the application's ABI and configuration. With a binary, the application must adopt the archive's ABI and configuration instead.

title: Diff 2: the float ABI is dictated by the archive
subtitle: Hard-float objects cannot link against this TX5 kernel

blocks.text:
# cmake/clang-arm-none-eabi.cmake
- TX5: -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=soft -fshort-enums
+ TX6: -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=hard
# TX5.6 PendSV: integer context only
  mrs   r12, psp
  stmdb r12!, {r4-r11}       @ no s16-s31, no lazy FP state
  ...
  mvn   lr, #2               @ EXC_RETURN 0xFFFFFFFD
blocks.label: Toolchain change plus disassembly of __tx_ts_handler in the archive

items: A hard-float task on this TX5 port would break: it saves no s16-s31 and always returns with a non-FP EXC_RETURN.
Stage 2 is therefore also the first point where FPU code becomes safe on M4.
The image attributes confirm it: TX5 has no FP_arch tag; TX6 M4 has VFPv4-D16 and AAPCS VFP.

title: Diff 3: vectors and the first context switch
subtitle: TX5.6 starts threads through SVC, TX6 does not

blocks.text:
# TX5.6 _tx_thread_schedule (from the archive)
  str   r1, [r0, #0x10]      @ SysTick CTRL |= ENABLE
  cpsie i
  svc   #0                   @ first thread starts in SVCall
# src/startup.S vector table
- .word DEMO_SVC_HANDLER     @ TX5: __tx_SVCallHandler
- .word DEMO_PENDSV_HANDLER  @ TX5: __tx_PendSVHandler
+ .word DEMO_SVC_HANDLER     @ TX6: fault_handler (unused)
+ .word DEMO_PENDSV_HANDLER  @ TX6: PendSV_Handler
blocks.label: Handler names are per-stage CMake defaults, validated as plain symbols

blocks.text: Leaving SVC at the TX6 default fault handler makes TX5 hang before the first thread runs. The verifier treats that as a timeout failure.

title: Diff 4: low-level init and the idle hook
subtitle: Contracts recovered from disassembly, implemented in MIT code

blocks.label: src/tx_initialize_low_level.c and src/tx5_wiced_port.c

items: The TX5 port objects reference _tx_thread_system_stack_ptr; the TX6 Cortex-M4 port sources do not use it.
The WICED idle loop calls tx_low_power_enter, which calls platform_power_down_hook(ticks to next timer).
A non-zero return is added to the kernel clock (tickless mode). Returning 0 keeps normal ticking.

title: Diff 5: a 4-byte configuration bug
subtitle: Found by the metrics, then made impossible to build

blocks.text:
[metric] sizeof_TX_THREAD=176        <- application's view
_tx_thread_create:  movs r2, #0xb4   <- archive clears 180 B
                    bl   memset
[metric] led_stack_high_water_bytes=1024   <- impossible
# cause: -Iinclude found the TX6 tx_user.h before WICED's,
#        dropping "#define TX_THREAD_USER_EXTENSION int errno;"
+ move TX6 config to config/tx6/tx_user.h
+ _Static_assert(sizeof(TX_THREAD) == 180U, ...);
[metric] sizeof_TX_THREAD=180   led_stack_high_water_bytes=196
blocks.label: Actual first Stage 1 run, root cause and fix

blocks.text: The kernel cleared 4 bytes past each 176-byte thread object. led_thread_stack follows led_thread in RAM, so its first fill word was zeroed and the stack scan reported a full stack. The functional test still passed: only the measurement exposed the corruption.
With a binary kernel, the header configuration is part of the ABI. It must be the configuration the archive was built with, and it should be asserted.

title: Diff 6: API and configuration details
subtitle: Small differences that break builds or change behaviour

items: The application dropped its own _tx_version_id declaration and uses the port header's.
Stack high-water is measured by scanning the 0xEF fill, which works on both kernels.
Thread resumption is checked with an application flag, not scheduler internals.

title: Diff 7: milliseconds versus RTOS ticks
subtitle: Keep units visible; avoid a silent tenfold delay error

blocks.text:
#define TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND 100   // tick rate used by both stages
#define LED_UPDATE_TICKS 25U
tx_thread_sleep(LED_UPDATE_TICKS);      // 250 ms virtual time
SysTick reload = DEMO_CLOCK_HZ / 100 - 1
SysTick_Handler -> _tx_timer_interrupt  // same symbol in TX5 and TX6
blocks.label: Timing integration, plus a measured tick invariant

blocks.text: The tested board clock constants are 25 MHz for MPS2-M4 and 32 MHz for MPS3-M55. The M85 build reuses the demonstration map and clock; a real M85 SoC must replace them.
QEMU icount is synthetic: 128 ns per emulated instruction. The tick invariant is a scheduler test, not a physical time or jitter guarantee.

title: Diff 8: preserve the held-button latch
subtitle: A subtle behavioural detail, checked at release as well as press

blocks.label: Application behaviour, identical on every stage

blocks.text: The verifier deliberately rejects a cycle-4 OFF result.

title: Diff 9: startup assembly under Clang
subtitle: A real encountered failure, with a trace-supported fix

blocks.text:
- sub r2, r2, r1   // Clang emitted sub.w, without updating flags
- beq copy_done    // branches on stale flags
+ copy_loop:
+     cmp r1, r2   // explicit end-pointer comparison
+     bhs copy_done
+     ldrb r3, [r0], #1
+     strb r3, [r1], #1
+     b copy_loop
blocks.label: Compared with the upstream TX6 example startup, not Broadcom source

blocks.text: QEMU traced a bus fault at 0x00080000 during the endless startup copy. The replacement uses explicit comparisons, copies .data, clears .bss and enables CP10/CP11.

title: Diff 10: TX6 security mode and BSP scope
subtitle: Scope down the first proof; make omitted features explicit

blocks.text:
# config/tx6/tx_user.h
+ #define TX_SINGLE_MODE_SECURE
+ #define TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND 100
+ #define TX_ENABLE_STACK_CHECKING
# boards/qemu.ld (all stages)
  CODE 0x00000000 512 KiB, RAM 0x20000000 32 KiB
  system stack 2048 B, 8-byte aligned; VTOR = demo_vectors
  PendSV/SVC priority 0xff, SysTick 0x40
blocks.label: Demonstrator configuration, not a production M85 BSP

items: Single-secure avoids exercising secure-stack paths without a non-secure image.
Do not infer a TrustZone security policy from a successful boot.
A real M85 SoC has its own memory map, clocks, IRQ routing, caches and MPU.

title: Diff 11: success is a checked contract
subtitle: Fail on missing, wrong or partial output

blocks.text:
+ require exactly one banner version, equal to the stage's
+     TX5: G5.6.5.2      TX6: 6.5.2.202603
+ verify the CPUID part number for the requested core
+ require queue / event / semaphore / mutex / pool self-test PASS
+ check all 10 button + LED rows and 9 intervals of 25 ticks
+ require explicit completion and QEMU exit status 0
+ reject timeout, wrong identity, wrong state or partial log
blocks.label: tests/run_qemu.py + 15 verifier unit tests

blocks.text: A TX6 image cannot pass as a TX5 run: the expected version is per stage and must match exactly. CMake also refuses a TX5 build on any core but M4, or with TX5_ROOT inside the repository.

title: The RTOS services really switch tasks
subtitle: A higher-priority worker must preempt, suspend, resume and signal

blocks.label: Condensed from the independently written service self-test

items: The progress flag is application state, so the check does not depend on TCB internals.
The timer wakes the sleeping LED task nine times through each kernel's real timer path.
Mutex and pool checks are basic operations, not contention or fragmentation stress.

subtitle: Recorded Stage 1 QEMU evidence, not a browser-side emulator

title: Memory chart: linked ROM
subtitle: Clang -O3; same application and service tests on every image

blocks.text: The TX5→TX6 delta is not pure kernel growth: the TX6 build enables error checking, preemption-threshold and a system timer thread, which the WICED release archive leaves out.

title: Memory chart: reserved RAM
subtitle: Include stacks and test infrastructure, not only global data

blocks.name: ram
blocks.caption: RAM = .data + .bss + 2 KiB system stack. Static task stacks are inside .bss.

blocks.text: TX5 M4: 5,624 B; TX6 M4: 6,964 B. TX6 adds a system timer thread and its stack; TX5 processes timers in the ISR. sizeof(TX_THREAD) happens to be 180 bytes on both kernels with these configurations.

title: Stack headroom is measured, not assumed
subtitle: The same fill-pattern scan on both kernels

blocks.name: stack
blocks.caption: Deepest LED-thread stack write under the test workload; 1024 bytes reserved.

blocks.text: TX5 M4 196 B, TX6 M4 224 B, TX6 M55 360 B. Differences come from the ABI, compiler code generation and each port's stack frame; they are not attributed to one cause.
Production worst-case paths, nested interrupts, FPU/MVE context and M85 behaviour still require stress and hardware validation.

title: Performance chart: emulator test cost
subtitle: Measure what was run, and say what the number means

blocks.name: host-cost
blocks.caption: Eight interleaved QEMU runs per image on this Windows host, using deterministic icount.

blocks.text: TX5 looks faster because its idle hook executes WFI, which QEMU skips to the next timer, while TX6 idles in a spin loop that QEMU must emulate. This is idle strategy, not kernel speed.

title: Histogram: repeatability of the host harness
subtitle: Samples are retained, not reduced to an unexplained mean

blocks.name: host-histogram
blocks.caption: Every plotted sample is in evidence/summary.json.

blocks.text: Use this to budget an automated test job and spot host variability. Do not turn the median differences into CPU or kernel performance claims.

title: Histogram: scheduler timing contract
subtitle: 216 measured intervals, all at the requested 25 ticks

blocks.text: The 100 Hz tick gives 250 ms in the configured virtual-time model on both kernels. Synthetic instruction time cannot establish physical sub-tick jitter.

title: What the M85 build proves
subtitle: Correct target attributes and resolved symbols, not execution

llvm-readelf -A build/m85/threadx_gpio_demo.elf
CPU_name: cortex-m85
CPU_arch: ARM v8.1-M Mainline
FP_arch:  ARMv8-a FP-D16      ABI_VFP_args: AAPCS VFP
MVE_arch: MVE integer and float
llvm-nm --undefined-only build/m85/threadx_gpio_demo.elf
# no undefined symbols
blocks.label: Actual attribute inspection; build uses upstream ports/cortex_m85/gnu

blocks.text: Clang compiled and LLD linked the unchanged application with the M85 port. The demo linker map and clock are not a production M85 SoC definition.
There is no M85 runtime, performance, power, PACBTI or mixed FPU/MVE correctness result.

title: The hardware acceptance gate
subtitle: Turn this proof into a product migration with explicit tests

rows: Vendor startup, linker map, GPIO polarity, clock tree, IRQ map
Preemption + nested IRQ + mixed scalar/FPU/MVE tasks; inspect saved context
TrustZone policy, secure gateways/stacks, MPU and optional PACBTI
On-silicon cycles, IRQ latency, deadline/WCET, throughput and energy, TX5 vs TX6
Peripheral, network, watchdog and low-power regression, incl. tickless idle
Licensing, SBOM, safety/change-impact assessment, traceable requirements

blocks.text: The proof reduces feasibility risk. It does not claim that Wi-Fi, TLS, OTA, safety certification or all application deadlines have migrated.

title: Reproduce the result
subtitle: Public source, pinned dependencies, raw evidence and automated checks

blocks.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/zuwasi/TX5-upgrade.git
# fetch the external SDK into TX5_ROOT (see README), then:
cmake --preset tx5-m4  && cmake --build --preset tx5-m4
cmake --preset tx6-m4  && cmake --build --preset tx6-m4
cmake --preset tx6-m85 && cmake --build --preset tx6-m85
cmake --preset m55     && cmake --build --preset m55
ctest --test-dir build/tx5-m4 ; ctest --test-dir build/m4
ctest --test-dir build/m55
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_verifier.py -v
python scripts/collect_evidence.py --repeats 8
blocks.label: Tools: Clang/LLVM, LLD, CMake, Ninja, Python and ARM QEMU

blocks.text: GitHub CI runs all four images, including Stage 1 against a fresh SDK clone. CI uses Linux packaged tools, so versions may differ from the recorded Windows run.
Only run firmware you trust with host semihosting enabled.

title: The technical conclusion
subtitle: A bounded yes, backed by executable evidence

items: YES: the application runs unchanged on the real ThreadX 5.6 Cortex-M4 kernel and on ThreadX 6.5.
YES: behaviour, service checks and every tick match between TX5 and TX6 on the same core.
YES: the same application compiles and links with the upstream Cortex-M85 port.
LEARNED: with a binary kernel, its ABI and header configuration are part of the contract.
NOT YET: M85 runtime and real-board BSP / timing / security qualification.

blocks.text: Next: choose the target M85 SoC and run the hardware acceptance suite, including a TX5-vs-TX6 cycle comparison on M4 silicon if that baseline matters.
